title: I like it, I don't like it
goal: Master the verb that works backwards — *piacere* — and talk about tastes, interests, and free time.
bekal: use *mi piace* and *mi piacciono* without mistakes
say you like doing things, not just things
talk about hobbies and how you spend your free time

dialogs.title: Dialogo — Che cosa ti piace fare?
dialogs.intro: Lunch in the park. A relaxed chat about what each of them likes — and one verb that works backwards.

lines.speaker: Giulia:
lines.text: Ti piace vivere qui a Bologna?
lines.id: Do you like living here in Bologna?
lines.literal: to-you pleases to-live here in Bologna?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Sì, molto. Mi piace la città, mi piacciono i portici.
lines.id: Yes, a lot. I like the city, I like the porticoes.
lines.literal: yes, much. to-me pleases the city, to-me please the porticoes.

lines.speaker: Giulia:
lines.text: E il cibo? Ti piace la cucina italiana?
lines.id: And the food? Do you like Italian cooking?
lines.literal: and the food? to-you pleases the cuisine italian?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Mi piace tantissimo. Ma non mi piace il caffè amaro.
lines.id: I love it. But I don't like bitter coffee.
lines.literal: to-me pleases very-much. but not to-me pleases the coffee bitter.

lines.speaker: Giulia:
lines.text: Ah, allora metti lo zucchero come tutti gli italiani.
lines.id: Ah, then add sugar like all Italians do.
lines.literal: ah, then put the sugar like all the italians.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Lo faccio già. E a te, che cosa piace fare il weekend?
lines.id: I already do. And you, what do you like doing on weekends?
lines.literal: it I-do already. and to you, what thing pleases to-do the weekend?

lines.speaker: Giulia:
lines.text: Mi piace camminare in collina e leggere al sole.
lines.id: I like walking in the hills and reading in the sun.
lines.literal: to-me pleases to-walk in hill and to-read at-the sun.

lines.speaker: Giulia:
lines.text: Guardare sì, praticare no. Odio correre.
lines.id: Watching, yes; doing, no. I hate running.
lines.literal: to-watch yes, to-practice no. I-hate to-run.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Neanche a me piace correre. Preferisco nuotare.
lines.id: I don't like running either. I prefer swimming.
lines.literal: neither to me pleases to-run. I-prefer to-swim.

lines.speaker: Giulia:
lines.text: A mia sorella piace nuotare. Andate insieme, no?
lines.id: My sister likes swimming. Why don't you two go together?
lines.literal: to my sister pleases to-swim. go together, no?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Volentieri! Ma solo se non nuota più veloce di me.
lines.id: Gladly! But only if she doesn't swim faster than me.
lines.literal: gladly! but only if not swims more fast than me.

notes: **Piacere works backwards.** *Mi piace la pizza* literally means "pizza is pleasing to me". The subject of the sentence is **the thing you like**, not the person who likes it. This is the hardest point in the unit — and the one people get wrong for life if they don't sort it out now.

**So there are only two forms: piace and piacciono.** One thing → *piace*. Several things → *piacciono*. *Mi piace la pizza*, *mi piacciono gli spaghetti*. What counts isn't how many people like it, but how many things are liked.
**Activities always take piace.** *Mi piace leggere*, *mi piace nuotare*, *mi piace camminare e leggere*. Infinitives count as one, even if you name three at once.
**What changes is the little word in front.** *Mi* (to me), *ti* (to you), *gli* (to him), *le* (to her), *ci* (to us), *vi* (to you all), *gli* (to them).

**For other people, use a.** *A Giulia piace nuotare*, *a mia sorella piace il caffè*, *a Marco piacciono i film*. The preposition *a* before the name is required — without it the sentence falls apart.
**Neanche a me** = "me neither". It pairs with *anche a me* ("me too", for positive statements). Answering *anche io* to *non mi piace* is a very common mistake.

**Odiare is an opposite that works normally.** *Odio correre* = I hate running — I'm the subject, regular word order. Same with *amare* (to love) and *preferire* (to prefer). Only *piacere* is backwards.
**Volentieri** = "gladly". The standard reply to an invitation, and much warmer than a plain *sì*.

grammars.title: Piacere — the backwards structure
body: Read the table from right to left: the thing liked is the subject.
after: The long form uses *a*: *a me piace*, *a te piace*, *a lui piace*, *a lei piace*, *a noi piace*, *a voi piace*, *a loro piace*. It's used for emphasis or contrast: *A me piace, a lui no.*
To negate: *non* goes first — *non mi piace*, not *mi non piace*.

⚠️ The most common mistake: *io piaccio la pizza*. That would mean "I am pleasing to pizza" — which makes no sense. The form *piaccio* does exist, but it means "I am liked": *Piaccio a Giulia* (Giulia likes me).

grammars.title: Saying how much you like something

head: Italiano
English
rows: I don't like it at all.

after: *Adoro* and *odio* are used much more lightly in Italian than their literal translations suggest. *Odio il lunedì* doesn't mean deep hatred of Mondays — just that Mondays are annoying.

blocks.text: ⚠️ *Giocare* and *suonare* both translate as "play" but can't be swapped. *Giocare* is for games and sports: *giocare a calcio*, *giocare a carte*. *Suonare* is for instruments: *suonare il piano*. Saying *giocare il piano* is a classic English speaker's mistake.

blocks.title: Asking and answering about tastes
items: *Che cosa ti piace fare nel tempo libero?* — What do you like doing in your free time?
*Qual è il tuo film preferito?* — What's your favorite movie?
*Ti piace…?* — Do you like…? → *Sì, molto.* / *No, per niente.*
*Anche a me!* — Me too! (for positive statements)
*Neanche a me.* — Me neither. (for negative statements)
*A me invece sì.* — Well, I do.
